syllabus.clause: role-playing dimensions (one date dimension, many roles)
outriggers; when each simplifies and when it complicates

items.item: A dimension sometimes has no content except its primary key, as with an invoice number once line items inherit the invoice's own descriptive keys
The degenerate dimension sits in the fact table with explicit acknowledgment that no dimension table exists for it; most common with transaction and accumulating snapshot facts
One physical dimension can be referenced multiple times in a fact table, each reference a logically distinct role
Each foreign key must refer to a separate, independent view of the shared dimension; these views are called roles
Low-cardinality flags and indicators from transactional processes can be combined into one junk dimension instead of many separate ones
A junk dimension need not be the full Cartesian product of every attribute's values — only the combinations that actually occur
A dimension can reference another dimension table; this secondary reference is called an outrigger
Outriggers are permissible but should be used sparingly; in most cases the correlation should be demoted to the fact table as separate foreign keys

expert.by: Claude (single session, written from the syllabus line and the fetched sources before storyboarding; not independent of the builder, so a later owner review should repeat it)

items.item: The degenerate-dimension predict (step 3) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that a key with no table behind it can't really be grouped on correctly; the reveal shows real GROUP BY results on a bare order number working exactly as any other key would

at.step: Predict: does a bare order number still work as a grouping key?

items.item: The outrigger predict (step 9) is red-teamed against the plausible wrong answer that an outrigger is purely a modeling nicety with no real cost; the reveal shows a genuine extra table touched on every query that needs the outrigger's own attribute

at.step: Predict: does an outrigger ever cost you anything to use?

items.item: All four measured reveals (steps 4, 6, 8, 11) run against real, disclosed throwaway tables built for this topic, not described hypotheticals — the grouping result, the two-role join, the three-vs-eight row count, and the three-table touch count are all executed, not asserted

The role-playing demonstration uses one single dim_date table referenced by two separate foreign keys, confirmed by counting the table's own row count once while joining it twice in two different roles in the same query
The junk-dimension demonstration explicitly computes the full Cartesian product (eight) alongside the three rows actually stored, so the saving is a measured comparison rather than a claimed one

Each pattern's own downside is stated honestly rather than omitted: the degenerate key gives up any descriptive attributes of its own, role-playing requires separately named views to avoid ambiguity, a junk dimension can still grow large if the flags are not genuinely low-cardinality, and the outrigger costs a real extra join, which is why Kimball's own material recommends demoting it to the fact table in most cases
The closing check (Prove it) applies the role-playing pattern to a new, undemonstrated case (a support ticket's opened/closed dates) rather than re-testing the exact order/ship dates from the reveal

The bridge from topic 10 (conformed dimensions and drill-across) is answered explicitly: this topic is framed as the patterns that exist because real dimensions often aren't the clean, well-behaved tables topic 10 assumed, and the handoff to the next topic (bridge tables and many-to-many) is confirmed by reading both CHAPTER.md entries side by side

Every number that appears on screen (the line counts, the row counts, the table-touch counts) traces to a literal constant in examples.py; every other quantity in reel.tsx is spelled in words, so no on-screen number is asserted without a matching computed value

The ligature characters in the quoted material ("deﬁned", "proﬁle", "ﬂags", "ﬂag") and the curly apostrophe in "attributes’" were copied character-for-character from the fetched HTML, verified by the word-for-word sources check rather than retyped from memory
